onboard/join: A teammate joins your project. The readme says: install Go and Node, then run the tests.
onboard/mine: You have one Go and one Node. They install newer ones. It happens to work for both of you.
onboard/break: Then the build server, with an older Node, fails on code that passes for you both.
onboard/global: The tools were installed by hand, for the whole machine, so every machine drifts its own way.
onboard/want: You want the project to say which tools it needs, and everyone to get exactly those.
mkshell/shell: A flake can say that. Beside packages, it can have a dev shells output: a development environment for each system.
mkshell/mk: Make shell is a small wrapper around make derivation. It gives you an environment to enter, not a package to install.
mkshell/pkgs: Packages lists the tools you want on path. Here, Go and Node.
mkshell/hook: Shell hook is a bit of bash that runs each time someone enters.
enter/enter: Nix develop reads that output and drops you into a new shell.
enter/where: Go is on path now, and it comes from the store. It is an ordinary store path, like any other.
enter/nothing: Nothing was installed globally. Another terminal, open at this moment, has no Go at all.
enter/exit: Leave the shell, and Go is gone from your environment.
enter/stay: But the store path has not gone anywhere. Next time you enter, it is already there, and the shell starts at once.
team/one: For one tool, once, there is nix shell. It puts rip grep on path, and that is all.
team/diff: Nix develop is for a project: the tools it lists, plus everything a build of it would have.
team/team: And since the flake has a lockfile, everyone on the project gets the same versions of all of it.
team/gc: One catch. Garbage collection deletes store paths that nothing needs any more, and nix store G C runs it. Your shell's tools are ordinary store paths, so they can go too.
team/root: A root is something that tells the collector to keep a path. Dash dash profile saves the environment to a file that acts as one.
